rendered: No amount of nickel, manganese or cobalt is reported as leaching into the Cyrene. The relative ratios of these metals in NMC622 stayed the same before and after separation, so the process does not leach them. The ICP-OES figures that back this are in the supplementary Table S1, which is not part of this document.[1][2][3] Only lithium leached. The paper states that lithium leaching from NMC622 occurred after recovery. It attributes this to the Cyrene molecule's ether groups, which attract lithium cations because ether is electron-donating. That causes lithium leaching and makes the high-Ni cathode more unstable.[4][5][6][7] The paper adds that the electrochemical degradation could be attributed to both the lithium leaching and possible surface changes caused by the Cyrene solvent.[8]
